newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU consumers' group lays out gene-maize criticisms.
newsitem.headline: EU consumers' group lays out gene-maize criticisms.

text.p: The European Commission should reject for now calls to approve Ciba -Geigy AG's genetically modified maize for market release in the EU, the European Consumers' Organistation (BEUC) said on Friday.
Jim Murray, BEUC's director, urged the Commission to throw out the maize approval application next week because of various fears held by his organisation.

These related to the modified corn's effects on bacterial resistance to certain antibiotics, to the risk that its release would weaken the effect of the existing, "environmentally friendly" insecticide Bt-toxin and to the possible increased use of the herbicide glufosinate, Murray said.

"BEUC calls on the Commission not to approve the Ciba-Geigy maize at this time since all our concerns have not been fully satisfied," he said in a paper addressed to the Commission and making specific reference to various scientific papers.
U.S. farmers grew their first crops this year of the gene-modified maize (corn) owned by Swiss chemical company Ciba-Geigy and cleared for release by the U.S. authorities.

The strain was developed to be resistant to the herbicide glufosinate, commonly marketed as Basta, and to carry the Bt-toxin to repel corn-borer pests. It also carries an antibiotic "marker gene" which BEUC said should be removed.
"The inclusion of the Bt-toxin in crops will impose a huge selection pressure on insects. It is likely that resistance in insects will develop," BEUC said.
Releasing glufosinate-resistant plants into fields raises the possibility of cross-breeding with wild, weed varieties which will then be more difficult to control, BEUC said.

The EU Commission is due to discuss and possibly decide on December 18 whether to allow imports of Ciba's modified maize, basing its decision on advice from its scientific committees on food, animal feed and pesticides.

Until then, it is illegal to market it in the EU, although environmental group Greenpeace says cargoes may have reached Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and Portugal, something which Spain and Portugal have denied.
European Union maize markets have generally ignored the Greenpeace protests over maize shipments believed to contain genetically-altered strains, traders said.
"I cannot imagine them denying U.S. maize entrance into the EU because it would cause a major bilateral trade row," one trader said on Thursday.
